newsitem.title: UK: British women tell of swimming from wrecked plane.
newsitem.headline: British women tell of swimming from wrecked plane.

text.p: Two British women described how they struggled out of their seatbelts and swam to the surface to escape from the wreckage of an Ethiopian passenger jet that crashed into the sea off the Comoro Islands killing 123 people.
Elizabeth Anders, 32, and Katherine Hayes, 31, were among just 52 people who survived the emergency crash landing of the hijacked Ethiopian Airlines flight on Saturday.
The plane broke into three pieces when the pilot ditched it into the sea just off the main island of the Indian Ocean archipelago after running out of fuel.
Hayes sent her family a fax telling of her dramatic escape.
"I was able to undo my seat belt and swam up to the surface," her brother Andrew said, reading from the fax.
"It is a miracle," he added. "She seems to be fine and have only minor injuries."
He said his sister may have survived because she was sitting in the smoking section at the back of the plane, which broke into pieces as it hit the shallow blue waters off an exclusive beach resort.

Chris Anders, Anders's father, said his daughter escaped the wreckage despite injuries. "She has got a fracture of her left leg, just above the ankle," he told Sky news. "Her hands are black and blue. They were under water and she managed to undo her seatbelt and got to the surface."

Kate Anders, her sister, said the two women were travelling together on a round-the-world trip. "I think we are all very lucky," she told ITN television. "For my sister and Katie Hayes, I can't believe it. It's a miracle."
"I just think of all those people who didn't make it," Anders's mother Patsy told Sky. "We are very, very lucky. I guess the grim reaper wasn't for our daughter."
The British Foreign Office said eight Britons were on board the Boeing 767. The fates of the six others were not yet known.
A British charity said a 43-year-old aid worker was among the six.
Andy Meakins, 43, from Beckenham in southern England, was working for the Christian charity Tear Fund in Addis Ababa, the group said in a statement.

"Andy was on the flight to attend a conference on the work of the church in Addis Ababa due to take place in Nairobi. He was completely committed to the needs of the poor and identified with the Ethiopian people," Stephen Rand, communications director for the organisation, said in a statement
"It is feared that a number of other mission and relief staff may have been on the plane to attend the same conference."
